headline: The ambassador's $100,000 card bill. A donor got asked.
summary: The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill before her confirmation hearing, promising access to officials in return. Marco Rubio refused to comment: "It's not the gospel." Two Democrats want an investigation. She denies wrongdoing.

cover_question.q: Why would a donor pay her bill?

cover_answer: The report says: for access. She says she did nothing wrong.
table_question: Is it a gift if they want something back?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A woman named Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks for America in Greece, far across the ocean. A newspaper says that before she got the job, she asked a rich man to pay a bill worth more than a new car, and promised to help him back. Her boss, Marco Rubio, won't say if it's true. She says she did nothing wrong, and the grown-ups are checking.
5-7.why: A bill the size of a car and a promise to help back is as far as seven needs to go.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them one bill, one rich man and one promise, and reads the whole story off that. Who Rubio is, and what a confirmation hearing is, can wait. Expect "did she pay it?" The articles don't say. Expect "is she bad?" She says no, and nobody has checked yet.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Kimberly Guilfoyle is the US ambassador to Greece. A newspaper says before the Senate approved her, she asked a Trump donor to pay her $100,000 card bill and promised him meetings with officials. A referee can't take money from one team. Rubio won't comment. She denies it.
8-12.why: A referee who can't take money is a rule they already enforce.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults apply the rules they set, so the script hands them the chain: a bill, a donor, a promise of meetings, and why that last link is the one that matters. The referee who can't take money from one team is a rule they already enforce. Expect "is she fired?" No. Rubio called her a strong ambassador on Wednesday.

13-17.script: Why would a donor pay her bill? The Wall Street Journal says Guilfoyle, days from her confirmation hearing, asked a Trump donor to wire her $100,000 and offered access to officials. Rubio: "It's not the gospel." Second: is a report true until checked, or false until proven?
13-17.why: Rubio's gospel line is a real argument about evidence. Let them take a side.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two things at once: the report is one newspaper's sourcing, and "not the gospel" is also a way of not answering. The script puts both on the table and asks who should check. Weighing evidence is a skill that gets practised, and this one has real stakes. Expect "is she guilty?" I don't know. Nobody has checked yet.

5-7.q: Why did she ask a rich man for money?
5-7.a: A newspaper says she owed a lot and promised to help him back. She says she did nothing wrong.

8-12.q: Is asking for money against the rules?
8-12.a: Asking isn't. Promising meetings in return may be. Two Democrats want it checked.
Speaks for the US in another country. Hers is Greece.

13-17.q: Why would a donor pay her bill?
13-17.a: The report says she offered access to officials in return. Money for a door.
Not yet. Two Democrats want an investigation. Rubio won't say. She denies it.
